title: Coaching Cut #20: The Premortem
author: Sarah Cottinghatt
summary: Sarah Cottinghatt, co-author of the forthcoming book Coaching for Adaptive Expertise, introduces the 'premortem' as a specific, codifiable coaching technique for overcoming the optimism bias - the natural assumption that a coachee's peak commitment during a coaching conversation will survive contact with the ordinary busyness of teaching life. Borrowing the concept from Gary Klein's 2007 'project premortem' (an inversion of the postmortem, imagining failure has already happened before it occurs), Cottinghatt demonstrates the technique through a worked coaching dialogue between coach Sarah and coachee Adam, in which Adam is asked to vividly imagine a specific future failure scenario ('it's Wednesday morning and you didn't script it') rather than being asked the generic, easily-deflected question 'what might go wrong?' She argues this concrete framing lets the coachee insert themselves into the imagined failure and identify real barriers more effectively, and pairs it with immediate action - having the coachee write the plan into their diary on the spot. Cottinghatt's broader argument is that coaching conversations themselves produce relatively little of the actual behaviour change; the premortem exists specifically to bridge the gap between a coachee's stated intention and their actual follow-through once they return to marking, meetings, and lesson planning.
points: Cottinghatt's core technique: the 'premortem' (Klein, 2007) has a coachee imagine that a specific future failure has already happened, working backward to identify concrete barriers before they occur, rather than relying on generic 'what might go wrong?' questions.

Her key design principle: specificity matters - asking a coachee to imagine a precise moment ('it's Wednesday morning and you didn't script it') surfaces real barriers, while a vague 'what could go wrong?' invites the coachee to fall back on the optimism bias and volunteer nothing.

The technique directly targets 'the optimism bias' - the natural assumption that a coachee's peak motivation during the coaching conversation itself will automatically survive contact with the ordinary busyness of daily teaching life.

Cottinghatt pairs the premortem with immediate action-locking: having the coachee write the planned action into their diary in the moment, since even the improved plan is vulnerable to simply being forgotten.

Her broader framing situates the premortem within a wider truth about coaching: 'the coaching conversation isn't where most of the learning happens; it just kickstarts the process' - follow-through, not the conversation itself, is where implementation succeeds or fails.
quotes: It's natural to assume our coachee will be motivated to implement their action step, especially as they're often at peak commitment levels during coaching. But when reality sinks in -- marking, meetings, lesson planning etc. --, predictable barriers to implementation get in the way.

A premortem flips that around. You imagine that failure has already happened before your coachee has even attempted to implement the step. This gets ahead of failure by anticipating likely barriers and planning to overcome them before they've even occurred.
By setting up the premortem in this way, Adam can insert himself into the future failure and think more concretely about what might have got him there.
If Sarah had just asked "what might go wrong?", it would have been easier for Adam to fall prey to the optimism bias and not volunteer any likely barriers.

It's way too easy for coach and coachee to assume it's plain sailing after the coaching conversation. But the coaching conversation isn't where most of the learning happens; it just kickstarts the process.
We risk it becoming tokenistic though if we simply end conversations with "what could go wrong?".
